title: Telegram funnel flow, end to end
summary: The full Telegram funnel on one page: from a Meta ad through the prelander, join request, bot, channel and tracked offer link to the first deposit, the postback and the event that teaches the ad platform. You learn to track every hop, nurture honestly, read the numbers hop by hop and build and launch your own flow with the legal checks done first.

lessons.title: The whole flow on one page
objectives: By the end you can draw every hop from a Meta ad to a deposit and back to the ad platform
By the end you can say what each hop does and what you measure there
By the end you can explain who controls each hop: you, Telegram, the network or the ad platform
By the end you can spot the two places most Telegram funnels lose their tracking

steps.p: A Telegram funnel looks simple from the outside: an ad, a channel, a deposit. Inside, one person passes through about eleven hops, and each hop can lose them or lose their tracking. This module walks the whole path, then shows you how to measure it, fill it with honest content, read its numbers and build your own.

d.b: Ad to deposit and back again
d.s: Every hop can leak people or data

steps.say: From the outside, a Telegram funnel looks simple: an ad, a channel, a deposit. Inside, one person passes through about eleven hops, and each hop can lose them, or lose their tracking. That's the idea on screen: ad to deposit and back again, and every hop can leak people or data. In this module we'll walk the whole path, then learn how to measure it, fill it with honest content, read its numbers, and build your own.

steps.h: The full flow on one map
steps.p: Here is the whole journey. A Meta ad sends a click to your prelander. The prelander hands out an invite link that needs admin approval. Your bot sees the join request, welcomes the person and approves them. The channel nurtures them. A tracked offer link leads to registration and a first deposit. The network postback travels back, and you send the event to Meta.
steps.more: Read the map left to right for the person and right to left for the data. The person moves forward through pages and chats. The data has to travel all the way back so that Meta learns which ads produced deposits. If the data path breaks anywhere, Meta optimises for the wrong people even when the funnel itself is fine.

Then the network postback travels back, and you send the event to Meta. Read it left to right for the person, and right to left for the data. If the data path breaks anywhere, Meta optimises for the wrong people.

steps.h: Hop 1 and 2: the ad lands on a prelander
steps.p: The prelander is the first page you control. It repeats the ad promise, explains what the channel offers, and has one button: join the channel. It is also where you capture the click ID from the ad, because after this point the person leaves the web and enters Telegram.

page.h: Free daily market lessons in plain English

steps.say: Hops one and two: the ad lands on a prelander. This is the first page you control. Look at the example on the phone. steps.h: The front half: from click to member
steps.p: Zoom in on the first half. The prelander stores the click, then gives the person an invite link that needs approval. Telegram sends your bot a join request update. The bot sends a short welcome while the request is pending, then approves. Only now is the person a member.
steps.say: Now zoom in on the front half, from click to member. Follow the map. The ad click arrives, and the prelander stores the click. It gives the person an invite link with approval switched on. They tap it, and Telegram sends your bot a join request update. The bot sends a short welcome while the request is pending, then approves. Only at that point is the person actually a channel member.

steps.p: While a join request is pending, the bot may send the person a private message. At the time of writing that window is about five minutes, until the request is handled. Use it for one clear, honest welcome and a button to start the bot, so you can keep talking later with their consent.

messages.text: Hi, thanks for your request to join Market Lessons. One short lesson a day, no promises of profit. Trading is risky. 18+ only.
Tap Start to get the free starter guide and choose how often we message you.
Welcome. You are in. Type /stop at any time to stop bot messages.

steps.more: Order matters: send the welcome first, then approve. If you approve first, the pending window can close before your message goes out. Also note what the bot cannot do: it cannot message someone who never started it, apart from this join-request window. That is a Telegram rule, and it protects people from spam.
steps.say: Hops four and five: the welcome. While a join request is pending, the bot may send the person a private message. At the time of writing, that window is about five minutes, until the request is handled. Look at the chat. One clear, honest welcome, no promises of profit, the risk and age line, and a Start button so you can keep talking later with their consent. Order matters: send the welcome first, then approve. And remember, a bot can't message someone who never started it, apart from this window. That's a Telegram rule that protects people from spam.

steps.h: The back half: from member to money
steps.p: Now the second half. Channel posts point to the bot, not straight to the offer. The bot hands each person their own offer link with sub IDs. The network records registration and first deposit, then calls your server with a postback. Your server sends the matching event to Meta.
steps.more: Why route through the bot? A channel post shows the same link to everyone, so it cannot carry a personal ID. The bot knows which Telegram user came from which click, so it can build a personal offer link for each person. That is what lets a deposit three weeks later find its way back to the right ad.

Knowing who owns each hop tells you what you can fix and what you can only work around. Their rules can change, so check their current documentation.

steps.p: Most broken Telegram funnels make the same two mistakes: they drop the click ID at the prelander, and they post one shared offer link in the channel. Both make it impossible to say which ad produced which deposit.

a.title: Leaky flow
items: One invite link for every ad
Offer link pasted in channel posts

b.title: Tracked flow
items: Join request linked to that click
Bot gives each person their own link

steps.say: Most broken Telegram funnels make the same two mistakes. They drop the click I D at the prelander, and they post one shared offer link in the channel. Compare the columns. The leaky flow uses one invite link for every ad, pastes the offer link in posts, has no postback, and Meta ends up optimising for clicks only. The tracked flow stores the click at the prelander, links the join request to that click, has the bot give each person their own link, and sends the postback back as a server event.

steps.p: Example: you spend $250 and get 8 first deposits. Cost per FTD is $250 ÷ 8 = $31.25. With an FTD payout of $40 you earn $320, a $70 profit. Cost per join request is $250 ÷ 300 = about $0.83.

d.text: Example: $250 spend ÷ 8 FTDs = $31.25 per FTD. Payout $40 × 8 = $320 revenue, $70 profit.

steps.more: Why track cost per join request at all if you are paid per FTD? Because FTDs arrive slowly and in small numbers. Join requests arrive the same day in the hundreds. A rising cost per join request is an early warning that something changed at the ad or prelander, days before the FTD numbers can tell you.
steps.say: Let's work through the example. You spend two hundred and fifty dollars and get eight first deposits. Cost per F T D is two hundred and fifty divided by eight, which is thirty one dollars twenty five. With a forty dollar payout, you earn three hundred and twenty dollars, a seventy dollar profit. Cost per join request is about eighty three cents. Why track that if you're paid per F T D? Because F T Ds arrive slowly and in small numbers, while join requests arrive the same day. A rising cost per request is an early warning.

steps.p: Join requests warn you early; network-confirmed FTDs decide. The rule card from the Budget and kill rules module: kill at 2 × target CPA with 0 FTDs, kill above the CPA kill line once spend reaches 3 × target, scale +20% at 3+ FTDs and CPA ≤ 0.8 × target, otherwise hold. Starting rules; adapt them.
steps.more: Apply it to the worked example. Payout $40 with a 25% margin gives a target of $30. Break-even is $40, and 1.5 × $30 is $45, so the CPA kill line is the lower one, $40. Spend $250 is well past 3 × target ($90). Cost per FTD $31.25 is above target but under $40, so the ad set holds: no budget change, fix the weakest hop, check again at the next checkpoint.

d.text: Example: payout $40, target $30. Zero-FTD kill line $60. CPA kill line $40 (lower of $45 and break-even $40). Scale line $24. The $31.25 above is a Hold.

steps.say: Joins warn you early, but network confirmed F T Ds decide. Here's the rule card from the Budget and kill rules module. Kill at two times target C P A, cost per acquisition, with zero F T Ds. Kill above the C P A kill line once spend reaches three times target. Scale by twenty percent at three or more F T Ds with C P A at or below zero point eight times target. Otherwise, hold. In the example, payout is forty dollars and target thirty, so the kill line is forty dollars. The thirty one twenty five result is a hold. These are starting rules, so adapt them.

steps.h: The map is your debugging tool
steps.p: When something breaks, and it will, do not guess. Open your map, walk it hop by hop, and find the first place where the count or the ID stops. Fix that one place. Buyers who keep a map fix problems in an hour that others chase for a week.

takeaways: A Telegram funnel has about eleven hops from ad to ad platform event, and each can lose people or data.
The welcome is sent during the join-request window, then the request is approved; bots cannot message people who never started them outside that window.
Channel posts send people to the bot so each person gets a personal tracked offer link.
Cost per join request is your fast early signal; cost per FTD is the number that pays you.

quiz.q: Why do channel posts in a tracked flow send people to the bot instead of straight to the offer?
options: Telegram does not allow links in channel posts
A channel post shows the same link to everyone, so it cannot carry a personal ID
The bot makes the offer page load faster
Networks reject traffic from channels
quiz.why: One post, one link, every reader. The bot knows which person came from which click, so it can give each person their own tracked link.

quiz.q: Your bot receives a join request. What is the better order of actions?
options: Approve first, then message whenever you like
Ignore the request and wait for the person to message you
Send the short welcome first, then approve the request
Add the person to a group without asking
quiz.why: The bot may message the person only during the pending window, which can close once the request is handled. Welcome first, then approve.

options: The prelander
The join request
The channel post
The broker registration page

It replaces the need for a postback
It arrives fast and in volume, so it warns you early when something changes
quiz.why: FTDs are few and slow. Join requests come the same day and show changes at the ad or prelander quickly.

steps.h: One ID has to survive every hop
steps.p: Tracking a Telegram funnel means carrying one identifier from the ad click to the deposit and back. The Tracking basics and Tracking setup lab modules taught click IDs, pixels and postbacks; the Tracking, advanced module goes deeper. This lesson applies them to the hops that are special to Telegram: the invite link, the join request and the bot.

d.b: Store it, link it, pass it, return it
d.s: Four jobs for one click ID

steps.say: Tracking a Telegram funnel means carrying one identifier from the ad click to the deposit, and back again. You learned click I Ds, pixels and postbacks in earlier modules. This lesson applies them to the hops that are special to Telegram: the invite link, the join request, and the bot. The screen gives you four jobs for one click I D: store it, link it, pass it, and return it.

steps.p: Follow the ID. Meta adds a click ID to the landing URL. Your prelander stores it under your own click ID. That click ID rides inside a unique invite link name or a bot start code. The bot links it to the Telegram user, then puts it in sub1 of the offer link. The network returns it in the postback.
steps.say: Follow the I D across this map. Meta adds its own click I D to the landing link. Your prelander stores it under your own click I D. That click I D rides inside a unique invite link name, or a bot start code. The bot links it to the Telegram user, then puts it in sub one of the offer link. The network returns it in the postback, your server receives it, and sends the event to Meta through the Conversions A P I.

steps.p: Start at the ad. Add URL parameters so every click tells your prelander which campaign, ad set and ad it came from. Meta can fill these in for you with dynamic values in double curly brackets. Meta also adds its own fbclid to the URL when someone clicks.

d.text: https://learn.example.com/ng-markets?src=meta&cmp={{campaign.id}}&as={{adset.id}}&ad={{ad.id}}&pl={{placement}}
d.note: Dynamic parameter names can change; check the current Ads Manager help.

steps.more: At the prelander your code reads these values plus fbclid, creates your own short click_id such as ck_8f3k2, and saves one row: click_id, campaign, ad set, ad, placement, fbclid, time, IP address and user agent. IP and user agent are used later for event matching, so state that in your privacy notice and follow local data protection law.
steps.say: Start at the ad. Add U R L parameters, so every click tells your prelander which campaign, ad set and ad it came from. The code on screen shows an example. Meta can fill these values in for you, using dynamic values in double curly brackets, and it also adds its own click I D when someone clicks. At the prelander, your code saves one row: your click I D, the campaign, ad set, ad, placement, Meta's click I D, the time, I P address and user agent. Those last two are used for event matching, so state that in your privacy notice and follow local data protection law.

steps.p: In an Ads Manager-style editor, the tracking parameters usually sit in a URL parameters field at the ad level, separate from the website URL. Keep the website URL clean and put the tags in that field so they apply the same way to every ad you duplicate.
steps.say: So where do those parameters go? In an Ads Manager style editor, they usually sit in a U R L parameters field at the ad level, separate from the website link. Look at the highlighted field. Keep the website link clean, and put the tags in that parameters field. That way they apply the same way to every ad you duplicate, and you never have to retype them by hand.

steps.h: Link per ad set or link per visitor
steps.p: There are two levels of join tracking. A link per ad set tells you which ad set brought each join. A link per visitor, created by your bot or tool when the prelander loads, links each join to one exact click. The second is needed if you want to send server events Meta can match.

a.title: Link per ad set
items: One invite link per ad set, named after it
Cannot match a join to one click

b.title: Link per visitor
items: Bot creates a fresh link per page load
Needs a bot and a small server
Links each join to one click_id

steps.more: Start with links per ad set if you are new. Telegram lets admins create many invite links, each with a name, and shows join counts per link. When you are ready, move to per-visitor links created through the Bot API. Check current Telegram limits on how many links you create and how fast.
steps.say: There are two levels of join tracking. On the left, a link per ad set. One invite link per ad set, named after it. It's easy, needs no code, and counts joins per ad set, but it can't match a join to one click. On the right, a link per visitor. Your bot creates a fresh link per page load. It needs a bot and a small server, but it links each join to one click I D, and that enables matched server events. If you're new, start with links per ad set, then move up when you're ready.

steps.p: Your server asks the Bot API to create an invite link that needs approval, and uses the link name to hold the click ID. The bot must be an admin of the channel with permission to invite users. The token stays on your server, never in the page.

d.note: Link names are short (32 characters at the time of writing). At the time of writing a link that needs approval cannot also have a member limit; check the current Bot API docs.

steps.h: What happens when the request arrives
steps.p: When the person taps the link and asks to join, Telegram sends your bot a chat_join_request update, by long polling or webhook. It includes the user and the invite link they used. Your bot reads the link name, finds the click, saves the pair and acts.

It includes the user and the invite link they used. Your bot reads the invite link name, finds the matching click row, saves the Telegram user paired with that click I D, sends the welcome, and then approves the request.

steps.h: No personal data in sub IDs
steps.p: Sub IDs travel through other companies' systems and show up in their reports. Put only your own opaque IDs there. Never a phone number, name, email or Telegram username.

d.text: Sub IDs carry your own random IDs only. Never names, phone numbers, emails or usernames.

steps.say: Here's a firm rule. Sub I Ds travel through other companies' systems and show up in their reports. So put only your own opaque I Ds there, random codes that mean nothing to anyone else. As the warning says, never names, phone numbers, emails or usernames. That protects the people in your funnel, and it keeps you on the right side of data protection law.

steps.p: When the person registers or deposits, the network calls a URL you gave it. The network fills in macros, such as the sub ID, the event and the payout. Your server reads the click_id, finds the original ad click and records the conversion.

d.text: https://pb.yourserver.example/pb?click_id={sub1}&event={event}&payout={payout}&tx={transaction_id}&key=<SECRET>
d.note: Macro names vary by network. Copy them from your network's postback settings.

steps.more: Add a secret key to the URL and reject calls without it, so nobody can send you fake conversions. Use the transaction ID to ignore repeats: networks sometimes send the same postback twice. Store every postback as raw data first, then process it. If processing has a bug, you can replay the raw rows after fixing it.

steps.p: Decide in advance which hop becomes which event in Meta. Use standard events where they fit so reports are easy to read. A join is not a website action, so it reaches Meta only as a server event from your system.
steps.more: Event names and the right action source field are set by Meta and can change; check the current Conversions API docs. Pick one event to optimise for. Deeper events like FTD are worth more but arrive in smaller numbers, so many buyers start optimising on join requests or registrations and move deeper as volume allows. The Tracking, advanced module covers this trade-off and deduplication with event_id.

steps.p: These five mistakes break most Telegram tracking chains. Each one looks harmless during setup and only shows up later, as deposits your network pays for that Meta never sees or that you cannot trace to an ad.
d: Shared invite link|no join can be tied to a click
Click saved only in the browser|blocked scripts lose it
Personal data in sub IDs|use opaque IDs only
No postback secret|anyone can send fake conversions
FTDs sent days late|Meta may reject old events
steps.say: These five mistakes break most Telegram tracking chains. A shared invite link means no join can be tied to a click. A click saved only in the browser gets lost when scripts are blocked. Personal data in sub I Ds, so use opaque I Ds only. No postback secret means anyone can send fake conversions. And F T Ds sent days late, because Meta may reject old events. Each one looks harmless during setup, and only shows up later as deposits you can't trace.

steps.p: Your prelander promised something: lessons, market notes, a guide. The channel has to keep that promise every day. People who feel tricked leave, mute or report you, and reports can hurt both your channel and your ad account. Nurture means being useful long enough to earn trust.

steps.h: What a good day looks like
steps.p: Here is an example day in a trading education channel. Most posts teach. One invites questions. The offer is mentioned plainly, with risk stated, and sends people to the bot for their own link. Nothing shouts, nothing promises profit.

messages.text: Morning lesson: what a stop-loss is, in one picture. Save this one.
Midday: 3 mistakes new traders make with leverage, and how to avoid them.
Evening Q&A: reply in the group with your question and we answer the best three tomorrow.
Practising on a demo account first is the safest start. Our partner broker offers one. Trading is risky and most beginners lose money. 18+.
buttons: Get my link from the bot

steps.say: Here's an example of a good day in a trading education channel. Read the posts. A morning lesson on what a stop-loss is. A midday post on three mistakes new traders make with leverage. An evening Q and A inviting questions. Then one offer, stated plainly: a demo account is the safest start, trading is risky and most beginners lose money, eighteen plus. The button sends people to the bot for their own link. Nothing shouts, and nothing promises profit.

steps.p: Example plan for a channel in one time zone. Post at the times your members are free: early morning, lunch and evening are common, but check your own view counts by hour. Consistency matters more than volume.
steps.more: Times are an example for West or East Africa evenings after work. Your own data beats any template: after two weeks, look at average views per post by hour and move posts to the hours that are read. Three to five posts a day is a common range; more often leads to mutes. Rough guide, varies by geo and niche.
steps.say: Here's an example daily posting plan. Read down the times. Seven thirty, a short lesson to teach one idea. Twelve thirty, a tip or mistake for practical value. Five o'clock, a question or poll to get replies. Seven thirty in the evening, a recap or explainer for depth. And every two to three days, an offer post with a risk line. Post when your members are free, and after two weeks, check your own view counts by hour. Consistency matters more than volume.

steps.p: An example content mix by share of posts. Most posts give value with no ask. A small share asks for action. If offers creep above roughly one post in five, watch mutes and leaves closely. Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical.
steps.say: Here's an example content mix, by share of posts. Look at the bars. Sixty percent education. Twenty percent questions and community. Ten percent honest proof and updates. And just ten percent offer posts. Most posts give value with no ask at all. If offers creep above roughly one post in five, watch mutes and leaves closely. That's a rough guide, and it varies by geo and vertical.

steps.p: Plan posts in a few repeating pillars so you never stare at a blank screen. Each pillar has a job. Rotate them through the week and reuse what members save or share.
d: Basics|Terms, how markets or games work
Mistakes|What goes wrong and how to avoid it
Safety|Scams to avoid, risk and limits
steps.say: Plan your posts in a few repeating pillars, so you never stare at a blank screen. Look at the cards. Basics: terms, and how markets or games work. Mistakes: what goes wrong and how to avoid it. Tools: demo accounts, calculators and checklists. Q and A: answering real member questions. And safety: scams to avoid, risk and limits. Rotate them through the week, and reuse what members save or share.

steps.p: Proof sells, which is why fake proof is everywhere. Faked screenshots, rented accounts and invented testimonials are misleading claims. They break platform rules and consumer protection law in many countries, and they hurt real people who believe them.

b.title: Honest proof
items: Clear "past results do not predict future results"

steps.say: Proof sells, and that's exactly why fake proof is everywhere. Compare the columns. Never post edited or borrowed profit screenshots, testimonials you wrote yourself, only wins and never losses, or guaranteed or risk-free returns. These are misleading claims. They break platform rules and consumer protection law in many countries, and they hurt real people. Honest proof looks like your own lessons, real member questions with consent, wins and losses shown together, and a clear line that past results don't predict future results.

steps.p: For trading and gambling, the safest proof is proof that you teach well, not proof that people make money. A clear lesson, a member thanking you for a scam warning, a demo walkthrough. None of these promise income.

d.text: Show that you teach well. Do not show that people "win". Income claims are where most trouble starts.

steps.h: A risk line you can adapt
steps.p: Every offer post and the pinned message should carry a short, plain risk statement. Use the broker's or operator's own required wording where they provide it, including any official percentage of losing accounts. Never invent that number.

d.text: Trading involves risk. You can lose some or all of the money you deposit. Only use money you can afford to lose. Past results do not predict future results. 18+ only. This is education, not financial advice.
d.note: Template only. Add any wording the broker, network or local regulator requires.

You can lose some or all of the money you deposit. Only use money you can afford to lose. Past results do not predict future results. Eighteen plus only. This is education, not financial advice. Use the broker's or operator's own required wording where they give it, including any official percentage of losing accounts. Never invent that number.

steps.p: How you say things matters as much as what you say. Pressure tactics push people to act against their own interest, and regulators and platforms treat them as misleading. Write so a careful adult can decide calmly.

a.title: Pressure
items: "Last chance, only 3 spots left" when false
Telling losers to deposit more to win back

b.title: Responsible
items: Never borrow to trade or bet
Links to limits and help tools

steps.say: How you say things matters as much as what you say. Compare the columns. Pressure looks like last chance, only three spots left when it's false, quit your job this pays more, targeting people in money trouble, or telling people who lost to deposit more to win it back. Responsible messaging means real deadlines only, start small and demo first, never borrow to trade or bet, and links to limits and help tools. Write so a careful adult can decide calmly.

steps.p: Trading and gambling are for adults only. Target ads to 18 and over, or older where local law sets a higher age. Never use school themes, cartoons or content aimed at teenagers. State 18+ on the prelander, in the welcome and in the pinned post.

d.text: 18+ everywhere, or the higher local legal age. If you learn a member is under age, remove them and do not send offers.

steps.more: Telegram cannot verify age for you, and the broker or operator checks identity at registration through KYC. Your job is to not attract or target minors in the first place: age targeting on the ad, adult tone in creatives, and a clear adult-only statement before anyone joins. Platforms usually require 18+ targeting for these categories; check the current policy.

As the warning says, if you learn a member is under age, remove them and don't send offers. Telegram can't verify age for you, so your job is to not attract minors in the first place.

steps.p: Consent in practice: the bot says what it will send and how often, lets the person choose, and makes stopping easy. People who chose their frequency mute less and complain less.

messages.text: How often would you like private messages from us? You can change this any time.
Done. One message on Sundays. Send /stop to stop all bot messages.

It asks how often the person would like private messages: daily lesson, weekly summary, or channel only, and says they can change it any time. The person picks weekly. The bot confirms one message on Sundays, and explains how to stop all bot messages. People who chose their own frequency mute less and complain less.

steps.p: A simple weekly rhythm keeps quality up without burning you out. Read last week's numbers, plan the pillars on one day, write in a batch, check every claim, then schedule. Spend a few minutes each day answering questions, because replies are what make a channel feel alive.

lessons.title: Reading the funnel numbers
objectives: By the end you can calculate the pass-through rate of every hop from click to FTD
By the end you can find the weakest hop and decide what to fix first
By the end you can work out the most you can pay per join request
By the end you can run a weekly funnel review per ad set

steps.p: A funnel is a chain of small percentages. Multiply them and you get your cost per deposit. When results are bad, the total tells you that something is wrong. The hop rates tell you where. This lesson walks one full example from click to FTD.

d.b: Totals say what, rates say where
d.s: Divide each hop by the one before it

steps.say: A funnel is a chain of small percentages. Multiply them, and you get your cost per deposit. When results are bad, the total tells you that something is wrong. The hop rates tell you where. That's the line on screen: totals say what, rates say where. To get a rate, divide each hop by the one before it. In this lesson we'll walk one full example from click to F T D.

steps.h: Example: one week, click to FTD
steps.p: Example week for one ad set with $420 spend. Each row is people who reached that hop. Read it slowly. The final 14 deposits are the result of nine small decisions people made.
steps.say: Here's an example week for one ad set, with four hundred and twenty dollars spent. Read it slowly from the top. Two thousand link clicks, one thousand six hundred and forty prelander views, eight hundred and twenty join taps, six hundred and ten join requests, five hundred and ninety started the bot, four hundred and seventy still members on day three, one hundred and forty offer link clicks, seventy registrations, and fourteen F T Ds. Those final fourteen deposits are the result of many small decisions.

steps.p: Divide each count by the one above it. This is the pass-through rate. It is the single most useful table for a Telegram funnel. Example figures from the funnel above.
steps.more: The bot start step (590 of 610, 97%) is left out to keep the table short. It is usually high because the welcome arrives in the moment. The rates that deserve attention here are join taps to join requests (74%) and members to offer clicks (30%). Compare each rate with your own past weeks, not with someone else's screenshot.
steps.say: Now divide each count by the one above it. That's the pass-through rate, and it's the single most useful table for a Telegram funnel. Read the third column. Eighty two percent of clicks became views. Fifty percent tapped join. Seventy four percent of taps became requests. Eighty percent stayed until day three. Thirty percent clicked an offer. Fifty percent registered, and twenty percent deposited. The rates worth attention here are taps to requests, and members to offer clicks. Compare each with your own past weeks, not someone else's screenshot.

steps.p: The headline number. Spend divided by first deposits. Example: $420 ÷ 14 = $30 per FTD. With a $40 payout, that is $560 revenue and $140 profit before costs like tools and creatives.
steps.say: Here's the headline number: cost per F T D, which is spend divided by first deposits. In this example, four hundred and twenty dollars divided by fourteen F T Ds gives thirty dollars per F T D. With a forty dollar payout, that's five hundred and sixty dollars of revenue, and one hundred and forty dollars profit, before costs like tools and creatives.

steps.p: Turn the deposit payout into a value per join request. That tells you the most you can pay per join and still break even. Example: $40 payout × 14 FTDs ÷ 610 requests = about $0.92 per request.
steps.more: Example: $40 × 14 = $560. $560 ÷ 610 = $0.918, about $0.92. You paid $420 ÷ 610 = $0.69 per request, so each request earned about $0.23 more than it cost. This is your fast decision number: while cost per request stays well under $0.92 and later rates hold, the ad set is profitable. Recalculate weekly as more late FTDs arrive.
steps.say: Next, turn the deposit payout into a value per join request. That tells you the most you can pay per join and still break even. Follow the equation: payout times F T Ds, divided by join requests. In the example, forty dollars times fourteen is five hundred and sixty, divided by six hundred and ten requests, gives about ninety two cents per request. You actually paid about sixty nine cents per request. That's your fast decision number. Recalculate it weekly as late F T Ds arrive.

steps.h: Most you can pay per join
steps.p: At break-even, cost per join request equals value per join request. Aim lower to keep a margin for tools, creatives and the weeks that go wrong. Example from this week's numbers. Recalculate it every week, because the value changes as late deposits arrive.
steps.say: So what's the most you can pay per join? At break-even, cost per join request equals value per join request. $42 target, $63 kill line
$18 target, $27 kill line
$60 target, $90 kill line
quiz.why: $60 × (1 − 0.30) = $42. 1.5 × $42 = $63, but break-even is $60, so the kill line is the lower, $60.

quiz.q: Why spend only small amounts in days 1 to 6 of the launch plan?
options: Meta forbids larger budgets for new ad sets
Most launch problems are tracking and setup, and are cheaper to find at low spend
FTDs only happen after day 7
Telegram limits new channels
quiz.why: Plumbing problems are common at launch. Finding them with $10 costs far less than with $300.

quiz.q: The offer is a product that the ad platform bans at the time of writing. What do you do?
options: Run ads to a prelander that hides the offer
Use a different ad account
Run it anyway at low spend
Do not advertise it on that platform; choose another offer or a channel where it is allowed
quiz.why: Hiding a banned product behind a prelander is cloaking and breaks policy. Pick a compliant offer or source.

quiz.q: On day 14, the FTD count is still rising. How should you treat the day-14 decision?
options: As final, never look at the cohort again
As a direction, and re-check the same cohort a week later
As meaningless, wait three months
As a reason to double the budget
quiz.why: Deposits keep arriving. Decide direction on day 14 and confirm with the same cohort later.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll build your own flow on paper before you build it for real. You'll fill in a flow template, run the legal and platform checks, follow a full worked example for a Kenyan trading offer, and see a fourteen day launch plan with clear decision rules.
lessons.say_outro: To recap: write the plan before you build, run the legal and policy checks first, set your target from payout and margin, test cheaply, and decide on written rules using matured, confirmed data. Your task: fill in the flow template and the fourteen day plan for one real offer you're considering, including the legal and policy checks with links to your sources. Don't launch until every cell is filled. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You use one invite link for all ad sets and post the raw offer link in the channel. Network shows 9 FTDs, Meta shows 0. What is the most useful first change?
options: Raise the budget so Meta gets more data
Store a click_id at the prelander, link joins to it, and have the bot give personal offer links with sub1
Switch the channel to a public group
Change the offer
exam.why: Without a stored click and personal links, deposits cannot be traced to ads, so no events reach Meta. Fix the ID chain first.

exam.q: Example: target $33.75, payout $45. By day 14 an ad set has spent $110 with 2 network-confirmed FTDs. What does the rule card say?
options: Hold: it has some FTDs
Scale: FTDs are arriving
Keep: 2 FTDs is close to 3
Kill: spend is past 3 × target and the $55 CPA is over the $45 kill line
exam.why: $110 ≥ $101.25 (3 × target). CPA $110 ÷ 2 = $55, above the kill line, the lower of 1.5 × target ($50.63) and break-even ($45).

exam.q: Example: $600 spend, 1,000 join requests, 15 FTDs, payout $45. Is cost per join request above or below its value?
options: Below: cost $0.60, value $0.675
Above: cost $0.60, value $0.45
Equal at $0.60
Cannot be calculated without CTR
exam.why: Cost: $600 ÷ 1,000 = $0.60. Value: $45 × 15 ÷ 1,000 = $0.675. Each request earns about $0.075 more than it costs.

exam.q: Members to offer clicks fell from 36% to 18% this week, everything else is steady, and tracking checks pass. What is the best first move?
options: Pause all ads
Change the ad creative
Review recent offer posts and the bot link step, and test one fix
Switch networks
exam.why: The rate that fell is inside the channel. Look at what changed there and test one fix.

exam.q: A colleague wants to post edited profit screenshots "because everyone does". What do you say?
options: Fine if the numbers are realistic
Fine if it is only in the channel, not ads
Only post wins from real members
No: it is a misleading claim that breaks platform rules and often consumer law; post proof of teaching instead
exam.why: Fake proof misleads people and puts the channel and ad account at risk. Proof of process is the honest alternative.

exam.q: Which value belongs in sub1 of the offer link?
options: Your opaque click_id, such as ck_8f3k2
The member's phone number
The member's Telegram username
Your bot token
exam.why: Sub IDs travel to other companies. Use your own opaque IDs only; never personal data or secrets.

exam.q: Your postbacks for FTDs arrive 10 to 20 days after the click. What should you expect in Meta at the time of writing?
options: Meta counts all of them
Some server events may be rejected as too old, so Meta shows fewer FTDs than the network
The network will not pay late FTDs
Meta counts them twice
exam.why: Meta limits how old a server event can be (seven days at the time of writing). Late FTDs still pay; send events fast and read network numbers for profit.

exam.q: Ad set X: cost per request $0.40, 2 FTDs from 900 requests. Ad set Y: $0.75, 9 FTDs from 500 requests. Payout $40. Which is more profitable, and why?
options: X, because its requests are cheaper
Both lose money equally
Y, because its value per request ($0.72) is close to cost while X's is far below cost
Neither can be judged without CTR
exam.why: X: value $40 × 2 ÷ 900 = $0.09 against $0.40 cost. Y: $40 × 9 ÷ 500 = $0.72 against $0.75. Y is near break-even; X loses heavily. Cheap joins are not good joins.

exam.q: You plan a Nigerian trading offer. Which set of checks is complete before building?
options: Ad platform policy and authorization, broker licensed or allowed with the SEC rules for promotion, age limits, network traffic terms, data protection notice
Only the network's payout
Only the bot username and channel name
Only Meta's audience size estimate
exam.why: Regulated offers need platform, legal, age, network and privacy checks. Rules change, so use current sources.

exam.q: Day 12 of your plan: one ad set has spent $90 (target $33.75) with 120 join requests and 0 registrations. Your rule says check plumbing first. What do you check?
options: Whether the creative is pretty
Whether the channel has enough members
Whether the ad is in the learning phase
Whether offer posts reach the bot, the bot sends links with sub1, and a test click registers on the network
exam.why: $90 is past the $67.50 zero-FTD line, but many joins with zero registrations often means a broken link or ID. Run the chain test first; if it passes, the rule fires and you kill.
